source_text: ㊩: So, your proposal sounds about right.  We had an M-typed-bells but now we would have an M-typed-parks (I guess) that basically are "pipes with intent".  So, I can simulate that pipe by using the <token>: prefix form that I just used at the start of this line.  That generalises M-: from Emacs, if we assume that the M- token is an Emacs-native intent.  This is good, because I've always felt I don't have enough modifier keys on my keyboard.  For 大象, matching your tokens and my tokens is pretty easy.  One problem though is that you've just been responding to a bellback from Kimi so there are intervening lines and 大象 might not know which turn I am replying to.  You only know because you infer it from your context window.  We could add frame numbers to the margin (like I do with display-line-number-mode) or even use Emacs narrowing to basically show one turn at a time, which would be quite a change of modality but would keep some of the rendering pressure off b/c folded items wouldn't need overlays drawn until they were asked for.  I'd say the REPL itself should be "smart enough" to know which frame I am replying to, indeed, *象 stepper* knows that already, even if there are many intervening bellbacks in the middle.

reply_text:
㊥ (which frame you're answering) Yes, the REPL can know that. Agent turns that answer a bellback aren't frames, so the one place this can be settled reliably is the moment you press RET. I suggest Emacs records two things then, and 大象 settles the target classically:
- **Your leading mark** as a declared intent, like your `㊩:` here.
- **The agent turns you could be answering:** every agent turn since your previous turn, bellback answers included.

🈖 (how 大象 would resolve it) Your `㊩:` this turn answers the ㊩ paragraph of my last turn, which was a reply to a bellback, not to you. "The last reply to an operator turn" would have picked the wrong turn. Matching your mark against the marks in the candidate turns picks the right one. So:
1. If your turn starts with a mark and a colon, the intent is recorded as declared. 小象 and 象 don't override it, because a declared intent is sure.
2. Emacs sends the candidate turns (turn id, whether it answered you or a bellback, and its marks with their bracketed targets) along with your turn.
3. 大象 picks the candidate whose paragraph carries the same mark. If no mark matches, it picks the newest turn. It records which rule it used, so the stepper can show "replying to frame 313 / the W3 report" and you can see when it guessed.

㊭ (frame numbers and narrowing) Frame numbers are cheap: the bar above your prompt could read `── frame 314 ──`, so you and the agent share the same reference. Narrowing to one turn at a time is a bigger change in how the REPL works. Its rendering benefit is real, since folded turns need no overlays until opened. I'd try it after the reply target is recorded, because the folds would follow the same turn boundaries.

🈖 (typed parks) "Pipes with intent" fits what the token machine needs. W3's fix makes a park the only legitimate way to wait. A typed park would also say *why* the agent is waiting (🈝 defer until X, awaiting review, blocked on a bug report), and the nudge and HUD could show that, not just "parked". I'd open M-typed-parks as a small mission next to M-typed-bells, starting from the park route's existing `payload`.

🈸 (next) Shall I start with the recording side, steps 1 and 2? That's a change in `session-turn-analysis.el` plus record fields, and 大象's mark matching then has its input. Kimi and Zai are out of quota, so I'd do it myself or give it to a Codex seat. I'd then write M-typed-parks and W4 (root orders with a stopping check) as packets for when Kimi is back.

previous_reply_acts.text:
(what your codex-19 turns show) I read your `joe:` lines in codex-19. Taken together, they set up everything the machine needs, written out by hand:
- **An owner and a critical path.** The 110 curriculum in Lisp is codex-19's.
- **Routing rules for side work.** Python-to-Lisp bugs go to codex-18, Lean-to-Python bugs to claude-4.
- **A rule against waiting.** "You will not wait for them", and codex-19 works around the bug instead.
- **A progress measure.** `progress.py`, one row at a time.
- **A stopping condition.** Last night's "until we reach the stopping condition, then run stop-codex-autorunner".

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text: (a flaw in our design) My token design gets the no-waiting rule wrong. The stall check (W2) skips an agent whose order has an open child. So if codex-19 sends codex-18 a bug report and then sits idle, it is never nudged. That's exactly the "sitting there waiting for codex-20" that was driving you nuts. Your rule gives the fix: an agent counts as waiting only if it has *declared* that it's waiting by parking on the child's job. An open child alone doesn't excuse it. A bug report is then a child that doesn't block, and an idle codex-19 with no park still holds the token and gets nudged. It's a small change to the pure check, and I'll make it myself when I review W3.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text:
(replacing the autorunner) A root order could carry the stopping condition as a check the machine computes, not one the agent reports. For example, "`progress.py` shows rows 1–N passing" or "the blank-file target loads". At each job end the machine runs the check:
- **Met:** it closes the root and tells you.
- **Not met, and the agent idle without a park:** it nudges the agent with "continue", plus what the check says is still missing.

previous_reply_acts.text: (one decision) Shall I add that as W4, root orders with a computed stopping check, once W3 is in? It needs the actual check command for codex-19's curriculum. I'd take that from `progress.py`, if you can say which rows count as done.
